Take a look at the clock on your wall.
Tick, tick, tick, every second
the same as the last.
For thousands of years,
many thinkers pictured the whole
universe the same way:
a great clockwork, wound up once
and running by fixed rules.
If the universe is a clock,
it seems natural to ask who built it.
So here is the question that has
followed humanity through every
age: does God exist?
Today we will not shout an answer.
We will do something stranger.
We will walk down into the smallest
scale of nature, where the clockwork
starts to look very different,
and see what quantum mechanics
really says about order,
cause, and design.
In eighteen fourteen, the French
mathematician Pierre-Simon Laplace
described a thought experiment.
Imagine an intellect that knew
the position and motion of every
particle in the universe,
and all the forces acting on them.
For such a mind,
he wrote, nothing would be uncertain.
The future would be as clear as the past.
Later readers called this mind
Laplace's demon.
It is the purest form of
determinism: every effect follows
from an earlier cause,
all the way back.
And for many people,
a universe that perfect seemed
to point to a designer standing
behind it all.
Long before Laplace, thinkers had
turned that feeling into arguments.
In the thirteenth century,
Thomas Aquinas listed five ways
of reasoning toward God in his
Summa Theologica.
Several of them lean on cause and design.
Everything that moves is moved
by something else, so there must
be a first mover.
Every effect has a cause,
so there must be a first cause.
And the orderly workings of nature
suggest a mind that guides them.
In sixteen eighty-seven, Isaac
Newton published his laws of motion,
and he himself believed that the
beautiful order of the solar system
came from an intelligent being.
Keep these three arguments in mind.
Quantum mechanics will test each one.
The first crack appeared in nineteen hundred.
The German physicist Max Planck
was trying to explain the glow
of hot objects.
The old physics gave nonsense answers.
Planck found that the numbers worked
only if energy comes in tiny
separate packets, which later came
to be called quanta.
He did not like what this implied,
and neither did many others.
But the idea kept working.
Over the next twenty-five years,
a new theory was built from it,
one that described atoms with
astonishing accuracy.
It also described a world that
behaves in ways our everyday senses
never prepare us for.
In October of nineteen twenty-seven,
many of the greatest physicists
on Earth met in Brussels for the
Solvay Conference.
Albert Einstein was there,
uneasy about the new theory.
Niels Bohr was there, defending it.
Einstein had written to his friend
Max Born the year before that
quantum mechanics was impressive,
but that an inner voice told him
it was not yet the real thing.
He was convinced, he wrote,
that God does not throw dice.
According to accounts passed down,
Bohr answered that Einstein should
stop telling God what to do.
Whether or not those exact words
were spoken, the argument was real.
It was about whether nature is truly random.
The experiment at the heart of
that argument is surprisingly simple.
Fire tiny pieces of matter,
electrons, at a wall with two narrow
slits, and place a screen behind it.
If electrons were little bullets,
you would expect two stripes on the screen.
But in nineteen sixty-one,
the physicist Claus Jonsson sent
electrons through slits and saw
something else: a pattern of many
light and dark bands,
the signature of waves overlapping.
Matter was behaving like a wave.
And that raised an uncomfortable question.
If each electron is a single thing,
what exactly is it interfering with?
It gets stranger.
In nineteen eighty-nine, a team
in Japan led by Akira Tonomura
sent electrons through the apparatus
one at a time.
Each electron landed on the screen
as a single dot,
like a particle.
But as thousands of dots piled
up, the striped wave pattern slowly appeared.
Each electron arrived as one point,
yet the pattern needed waves.
In standard quantum theory,
the electron is described by a
wave of possibilities that spreads
through both openings.
Many physicists put it loosely
by saying the electron goes through
both slits.
How to picture that is still debated.
The pattern itself is a measured fact.
Now add a detector at the slits
to find out which path each electron takes.
The moment the experiment records
that information, the striped
pattern disappears, and two plain
bands remain.
Learning the path destroys the interference.
Does this mean a human mind changes
reality just by looking?
That is the most popular
misunderstanding in all of physics.
What matters is not a person's attention.
What matters is whether the path
information gets recorded in the
physical world.
Even an automatic detector that
nobody ever reads is enough to
wash the pattern away.
This is why physicists use the
word measurement, not mind.
In real laboratories, the observer
is a photon detector,
a bit of gas,
a speck of dust,
a piece of glass.
Nobody has found an experiment
showing that consciousness plays
a special role.
This matters for our question,
because some people hoped the
observer was a doorway for God,
an eternal watcher keeping the world solid.
The experiments simply do not point that way.
Reality at the small scale is
strange, but it does not need a
person, or a deity,
to look at it before it behaves.
In nineteen twenty-seven, the German
physicist Werner Heisenberg
published the uncertainty principle,
and the same year Earle Kennard
gave it its exact mathematical form.
It says that the position of a
particle and its momentum cannot
both be sharply defined at once.
The more tightly you pin one down,
the fuzzier the other becomes.
Many people think this is only
about clumsy instruments disturbing
the particle.
It goes deeper.
In standard quantum theory,
a particle simply does not have
a perfectly sharp position and
a perfectly sharp momentum together.
The fuzziness belongs to nature
itself, and it has been confirmed
in countless experiments.
Now think about Laplace's demon again.
It needed to know the exact position
and momentum of every particle.
If the uncertainty principle is
built into nature, that perfect
knowledge is not just hard,
it is not available at all.
What does that do to an all-knowing God?
Thinkers answer in different ways.
Some argue that an all-knowing
being knows everything that can
be known, and a value that does
not exist is nothing to know.
Others reject the whole comparison.
And some physical theories add
hidden details underneath.
So this is a real philosophical debate.
Physics does not settle it,
but it does change what the debate is about.
Here is another place where nature
seems to roll dice.
Take an unstable atom,
such as carbon-fourteen, the kind
archaeologists use to date ancient bones.
Physics can tell you the chance
that it decays during the next
hour with great precision.
But it cannot tell you when that
one atom will go.
Two identical atoms sitting side
by side can decay minutes or
millions of years apart.
In standard quantum theory,
there is no hidden clock inside
the nucleus and no trigger that
can be found.
The randomness appears to be real.
And a chain of causes,
one domino striking the next,
no longer describes how the smallest
things behave.
Look at how different the clocks
of decay can be.
The half-life is the time in which
half of a large sample of atoms
will have decayed.
For radon-two-twenty-two, it is
about three point eight days.
For carbon-fourteen, it is about
fifty-seven hundred thirty years.
And for uranium-two-thirty-eight,
it is about four point four seven
billion years, close to the age
of the Earth itself.
Yet in every case,
the half-life says nothing about
any single atom.
The group behaves with iron regularity.
The individual atom keeps its own
timing a secret, even from the equations.
Now for an honest correction.
Quantum mechanics predicts its
results magnificently, but
physicists still disagree about
what it means.
Some readings keep true randomness.
Others do not.
In the de Broglie and Bohm version,
particles have definite positions,
guided by a wave,
and the future is determined,
though the guiding wave is nonlocal
and the hidden details can never be seen.
In the many-worlds version,
nothing is random at all,
and every outcome happens.
So quantum theory does not force
a universe of pure chance.
What it does is end the simple,
local, mechanical clockwork that
Laplace imagined.
That is a smaller claim than some
headlines make, and a more accurate one.
Now the vacuum, the emptiest place there is.
In quantum field theory,
empty space is not a blank stage.
It has a lowest energy state,
and its fields are never perfectly still.
In nineteen forty-seven, Willis
Lamb and Robert Retherford measured
a tiny shift in the energy levels
of hydrogen that the old theory
could not explain, and quantum theory could.
In nineteen forty-eight, Hendrik
Casimir predicted that two metal
plates in a vacuum would feel a
faint force, and in nineteen
ninety-seven, Steve Lamoreaux
measured it precisely.
So the vacuum is a physical thing
with real effects, not an absence.
Religions and philosophers have
long said that nothing comes from nothing.
How does a busy vacuum bear on this?
Since the nineteen seventies,
some physicists, such as Edward
Tryon and Alexander Vilenkin,
proposed that the universe could
arise from a quantum fluctuation
or a tunneling event.
These are speculative ideas,
not established facts.
And the nothing in them is a
quantum state with laws and fields,
not the philosophical nothing,
which critics point out.
What physics honestly says is this:
we do not know what,
if anything, came before the Big Bang.
Quantum theory gives us ways to
ask the question.
It has not yet given us the answer.
In nineteen thirty-five, Einstein,
Boris Podolsky, and Nathan Rosen
published a famous paper asking
whether quantum mechanics could
be a complete description of reality.
They pointed to a strange case:
two particles prepared together,
then separated, whose measured
properties stay linked no matter the distance.
We now call this entanglement.
Einstein disliked it.
In a later letter,
he called it spooky action at a distance.
He suspected the particles carried
hidden instructions from the start,
like two sealed envelopes holding
matching cards.
For three decades, nobody could
tell whether he was right.
It looked like a debate that could
never be settled by experiment.
Then, in nineteen sixty-four,
the Northern Irish physicist John
Stewart Bell found a way.
He showed that any theory of local
hidden instructions must obey a
mathematical limit on how strongly
the measurements can agree.
Quantum theory predicted the limit
would be broken.
In the early nineteen seventies,
John Clauser and Stuart Freedman
ran the first test.
In nineteen eighty-two, Alain Aspect
closed more gaps.
In twenty fifteen, three groups
ran loophole-free tests.
All of them found the limit broken,
just as quantum theory predicted.
In twenty twenty-two, Aspect,
Clauser, and Anton Zeilinger shared
the Nobel Prize in Physics for this work.
What did these experiments really rule out?
Local realism: the idea that
particles carry definite properties
of their own, and that nothing
can influence them faster than light.
At least one of those two
assumptions has to go.
Some physicists drop definite
properties before measurement.
Others accept a kind of nonlocal
connection, as in the Bohm picture.
But here is the key point.
Entanglement cannot be used to
send a message faster than light,
and Einstein's relativity survives.
So the universe is more tightly
connected than the clockwork picture
allowed, but it is not lawless,
and it is not telepathy.
If tiny things are so strange,
why does a chair look solid?
A big part of the answer is
decoherence, worked out by H.
Dieter Zeh in nineteen seventy
and developed by Wojciech Zurek and others.
When a quantum system interacts
with its surroundings, with air
molecules and photons, its delicate
wave behavior leaks out into the
environment, very fast.
The result looks like ordinary,
definite, classical behavior.
No mind is needed,
only countless blind collisions.
A fair note: many physicists say
decoherence explains why we do
not see superpositions in daily
life, but not, by itself,
why one single outcome happens.
That deeper question is still open.
This brings us back to the cosmic observer.
The idea that things exist only
while perceived is old.
The eighteenth-century philosopher
George Berkeley argued it,
and said God's constant perception
keeps the world in being.
Some people now borrow quantum
language to defend that picture.
But the physics does not require it.
Decoherence works the same in a
laboratory, in a gas cloud,
and in deep space where nobody is looking.
So quantum mechanics gives no
support to an observer-God that
holds reality together.
It also does not rule out the
idea as philosophy.
It simply makes the physical
argument unnecessary.
Then there is the most famous animal
in physics.
In nineteen thirty-five, Erwin
Schrodinger described a cat sealed
in a box with a radioactive atom,
a detector, and a vial of poison.
If the atom decays,
the cat dies.
Quantum theory, applied naively,
would describe the cat as both
alive and dead until the box is opened.
Schrodinger did not offer this as a fact.
He offered it as a warning:
a way to show how strange the
theory sounds when it is stretched
to everyday objects.
No real cat is ever found half alive.
Decoherence explains why the box
acts like a measuring device almost instantly.
In nineteen fifty-seven, Hugh
Everett the Third proposed a radical idea.
What if the wave function never
collapses at all?
Instead, every possible outcome
happens, each in its own branch
of an ever-growing reality.
This many-worlds view takes the
equations at face value,
and it has serious supporters.
It also has serious critics,
and no experiment can yet tell
it apart from its rivals.
So when someone says physics has
proven there are endless copies
of you, be careful.
That is an interpretation,
one among several.
What is solid is the mathematics.
What it means, philosophically
and theologically, is still argued over.
In nineteen sixty-one, the physicist
Eugene Wigner, who later won a
Nobel Prize, posed a puzzle.
A friend measures a quantum system
inside a sealed laboratory.
For the friend, there is one definite result.
But for Wigner, outside,
the whole lab might still be
described as a superposition.
In twenty nineteen, researchers
in Scotland built a small version
of this with entangled photons.
Their results are consistent with
the claim that different observers
can disagree about facts,
but only under certain assumptions,
and physicists still argue about
those assumptions.
The honest summary is that nobody
knows whether there is one objective
story of the world.
Picture a casino with billions
of roulette wheels.
Each spin is unpredictable.
Yet over trillions of spins,
the totals become so regular that
the casino can predict its profit
to the dollar.
Something like this happens in matter.
Individual atoms behave
probabilistically, but a chair
contains an unimaginable number
of them, so their average behavior is steady.
That is part of why the large
world looks like Laplace's clock.
For the design argument,
this is interesting.
Stable order does not need every
detail to be fixed in advance.
Whether that order still points
to a designer is a question physics
cannot answer, but it does show
the order is not fragile.
Quantum randomness may even have
shaped the sky.
The leading theory of the early
universe, cosmic inflation, proposes
that tiny quantum fluctuations
were stretched to enormous size,
and became the seeds of galaxies.
In nineteen ninety-two, NASA's
COBE satellite detected faint
ripples in the afterglow of the
Big Bang, differing by only about
one part in one hundred thousand.
John Mather and George Smoot
received the Nobel Prize for this
work in two thousand six.
Inflation itself is not yet
confirmed, and it remains a leading
idea, not a certainty.
But the ripples are real.
The great web of galaxies seems
to grow from the smallest, quietest wobbles.
Could quantum effects reach into biology?
Per-Olov Lowdin suggested in
nineteen sixty-three that a proton
in DNA might tunnel between
positions, causing a copying mistake.
Recent computer models say this is plausible.
But it is a hypothesis.
We do not know how often it
happens in living cells, if at all.
What we do know is that most
mutations come from ordinary
sources: copying errors, chemical
damage, and radiation.
And evolution works through natural
selection, which is not random
at all, since it keeps what survives.
So be careful with claims that
evolution runs on quantum accidents.
Perhaps a few contribute.
The science is still open.
Many believers hoped quantum
randomness would rescue free will.
If the world is not fully
determined, perhaps people can truly choose.
But think about it.
If a choice is decided by a
random event, it is not chosen
by you, it just happens.
Free will would need something
more than chance.
Philosophers still disagree about this.
Some argue that free will fits
with determinism, and others that
it needs indeterminism.
And we have no good evidence that
single quantum events steer our
decisions at all.
Quantum physics, then, neither
saves free will nor destroys it.
It simply does not settle the matter.
Now a warning.
Since the nineteen seventies,
many books and seminars have claimed
that quantum physics proves the
power of positive thinking,
or that your thoughts shape physical reality.
Experiments do not support those claims.
The observer in physics is any
physical system that records
information, not a hopeful state of mind.
Quantum entanglement does not prove
cosmic love, and it cannot carry telepathy.
This matters for our question as well.
Bad arguments for God and bad
arguments against God both borrow
the same quantum language.
The way to tell a good argument
from a bad one is to ask
what the experiment actually measured.
In nineteen seventy-four, Stephen
Hawking showed that quantum effects
near the edge of a black hole
should make it glow faintly.
This is now called Hawking radiation.
The black hole slowly loses energy,
and over unimaginable time,
it should evaporate.
For a black hole as heavy as
the Sun, that would take far longer
than the current age of the
universe, about thirteen point
eight billion years.
Nobody has detected this radiation
directly from a real black hole,
so it remains a theoretical prediction.
But it is a good example of
quantum theory and gravity meeting,
and it is one of the places
where physicists are still hunting
for the deeper truth.
What is the end of the story?
The leading forecast, based on
today's observations of accelerating
expansion, is a very long, cold fade.
Stars will form for a long while,
then run out of fuel.
The smallest stars, the red dwarfs,
can burn for trillions of years.
After that, only remnants will
remain: dim embers, black holes,
and thin, cold space.
Scientists call this possibility
the heat death of the universe.
It is a prediction,
not a certainty, and new discoveries
could change it.
Religions often promise a dramatic ending.
The physics suggests a quiet one,
and it asks us to find meaning
in the short, bright time we have.
So, does quantum mechanics prove
that God does not exist?
No, and it is important to say so plainly.
Science studies the natural world,
using measurements and tests.
It can challenge particular
arguments, such as a perfectly
predictable universe, a simple
chain of causes, or a fragile design.
It cannot rule out every idea of
God, and physicists themselves
hold a wide range of views.
A famous story says that Laplace
told Napoleon he had no need of
that hypothesis.
Even if the story is only an
anecdote, it captures a real point.
Physics explains how nature works
without invoking God.
Whether that is the end of the
question is something physics leaves to you.
Let us return to where we began.
You still have a clock on the
wall, but now you know the world
beneath it is far stranger than clockwork.
Almost every atom in your body
heavier than hydrogen was forged
inside stars, long before the Earth existed.
We are the universe,
grown able to ask about itself.
Tonight, look up at the stars and wonder.
Subscribing and liking is what
lets Miya's Lab keep asking the
next strange question.
Whatever you conclude about God,
keep your curiosity honest,
and keep it brave.
The truth, as far as we can
reach it, is deeper than any
comfortable story.
